content: Metamizole sodium is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that was historically used as a potent analgesic and antipyretic. It is more commonly recognized under the names Dipyrone, Analgin, and Novalgin. The compound was first synthesized in 1920 by the German pharmaceutical company Hoechst AG, with mass production commencing in 1922. For decades, it was widely available globally until the 1970s, when it was discovered to carry a risk of inducing agranulocytosis, a severe and potentially life-threatening condition characterized by a marked reduction in neutrophils, a type of white blood cell. This revelation led to significant controversy regarding the drug's safety profile, with some countries banning it outright or restricting its use to prescription-only status. Dr. Anthony Wong from the University of São Paulo, Brazil, commented in a WHO newsletter that recent studies estimate the incidence of metamizole-induced agranulocytosis to range between 0.2 and 2 cases per million person-days of use. Among these cases, approximately 7% are fatal, assuming patients have access to prompt medical care. To contextualize this risk, in a population of 300 million where every individual takes the drug once a month, this would translate to an estimated 50 to 500 deaths annually. While this risk is relatively low compared to other drugs, such as clozapine, which is at least 50 times more likely to cause agranulocytosis, the perceived risk in the 1970s was considered excessive for an over-the-counter medication, especially given the availability of safer alternatives like aspirin and ibuprofen. A 2002 study conducted in Northern Sweden suggested that the risk of agranulocytosis during metamizole therapy might be significantly higher than Dr. Wong's estimates, with calculated risks of approximately 1 in 31,000 for hospitalized patients and 1 in 1,400 for outpatients. Metamizole has been banned in several countries, including Sweden (1974), the United States (1977), and more than 30 others, such as Japan, Australia, and parts of the European Union. In some of these countries, it is still occasionally used in veterinary medicine. In Germany, the drug is available only by prescription. Despite these restrictions, some pharmaceutical companies, such as Hoechst and Merck, continue to develop and market metamizole-containing products in certain regions. In Sweden, the ban was briefly lifted in 1995 but reinstated in 1999, and the drug was subsequently removed from the market again a few years later. In contrast, metamizole remains widely available over-the-counter in many parts of the world, including Spain, Mexico, India, Brazil, Russia, Bulgaria, Romania, Israel, and several developing countries. It is one of the most commonly used analgesics in these regions and plays a significant role in self-medication. For instance, in Russia, metamizole and its derivatives account for 80% of the over-the-counter analgesic market, compared to just 2.5% for ibuprofen. In Brazil, metamizole products, such as Novalgina, are sold over-the-counter but include warnings advising against use in individuals under 19 years of age and provide information on the early detection and treatment of agranulocytosis. Although the Brazilian government has not banned the drug, its use has declined in recent years as pharmaceutical companies and healthcare providers have promoted alternatives like aspirin, paracetamol, and ibuprofen, particularly for pediatric use. However, metamizole remains widely used among adults in Brazil, with popular products including Buscopan Plus (marketed as Buscopan Composto), Novalgina, and Neosaldina. Generic dipyrone is also readily available. Metamizole briefly garnered attention in the United States in 2001 when a Latino immigrant child was admitted to a Salt Lake City clinic with agranulocytosis. It was discovered that the drug, despite being banned, was still widely available in Latino stores and remained popular among Mexican immigrants. The ongoing LATIN Study, an international multicenter case-control study, is investigating the incidence of agranulocytosis in Latin America and the role of metamizole in its development. Metamizole is marketed under various brand names worldwide. In Brazil, these include Novalgina, Neosaldina, Sedalgina, Doridina, Migranette, Benegrip, Anador, Magnopyrol, Conmel, Difebril, Termopirona, Dipifarma, Termosil, Dorona, Hynalgin, and Lisador. In Bulgaria, it is sold as Proalgin and Analgin. In Croatia, it is known as Analgin, while in Finland, it is marketed as Litalgin. In Germany, it is available as Novalgin, Analgin, Berlosin, Metalgin, Metamizol-Puren, and Novaminsulfon. Hungary markets it as Algopyrin, and in India, it is sold as Novalgin. In Israel, it is known as Optalgin, and in Italy, as Novalgina. Macedonia and Serbia both market it as Analgin. In Mexico, it is sold as Neo-Melubrina, while in Poland, it is known as Pyralgina. Romania markets it as Algocalmin, Novocalmin, Algozone, and Nevralgin. In Russia and Bulgaria, it is available as Tempalgin, a combination drug containing metamizole. In Slovenia, it is sold as Analgin, while in Spain, it is marketed as Nolotil. In Switzerland and Turkey, it is sold as Novalgin, and in Venezuela, it is known as Novalcina.
